findings.description: No server_side_encryption_configuration is defined, so objects in this bucket are stored unencrypted at rest (or rely on defaults that may not enforce encryption), risking data exposure if underlying storage is compromised.

No 'acl' attribute is set and no aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block is applied, leaving the bucket's access control ambiguous and potentially defaulting to a less restrictive posture; combined with force_destroy=true, sensitive report data could be exposed or destroyed without protection.
This bucket stores ledger exports (likely sensitive financial data) but has no server_side_encryption_configuration block, leaving data unencrypted at rest.
No logging configuration is set for this sensitive ledger data bucket, preventing audit visibility into access patterns, which weakens detection of unauthorized access.
No server_side_encryption_configuration is defined for this bucket, so model artifacts are stored unencrypted at rest.
No server_side_encryption_configuration is defined, leaving operational runbook data (which may contain sensitive internal procedures/credentials references) unencrypted at rest.

The bucket uses the 'log-delivery-write' canned ACL, which grants the S3 log delivery group write and read-acp permissions; combined with force_destroy=true, this increases risk of unauthorized write/tampering or deletion of audit logs if not tightly scoped.
force_destroy = true allows the bucket and all its contents to be deleted via a terraform destroy/apply without recovery, which can be leveraged to destroy evidence or sensitive report data.

The object is uploaded without specifying server-side encryption (kms_key_id or server_side_encryption), and the destination bucket also lacks default encryption, so this vendor roster file (potentially containing PII) is stored unencrypted.
